clue.text: Writing on the wall for short fat git behaving badly

indicators.note: letters that behave badly refuse to stay in their proper order, so the fodder is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: short means cut short, so the phrase 'fat git' loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written, then trimmed

explanation.surface: Someone scrawls an insult about an unpleasant overweight person on a wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims FAT GIT to FATGI; 'behaving badly' rearranges it with FOR. A git is British slang for an unpleasant person.
explanation.definitionFit: A graffito is the singular of graffiti, a single piece of scribbled writing on a public wall.

clue.text: Unusually formed geographical features seen from this winding road

indicators.note: a winding course twists about, so the letters of 'this' are rearranged

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway, written MI in crosswords

explanation.surface: Peculiar landforms can be spotted from this twisty road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'winding' rearranges THIS to ISTH. 'Unusually formed' belongs to the definition: the plural form with -i is the irregular one. The M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrow land bridges joining two larger masses are landforms, and this Latin-style plural is the rarer form of the word.

clue.text: Scottish conservationists restrained by person who's trying to kill animals

indicators.note: something restrained by another is held within it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a person is a human being
NTS is the National Trust for Scotland, which conserves historic buildings and land

explanation.surface: Scottish conservation workers detain a hunter going after wildlife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'restrained by' signals the container. 'person' gives the wordplay, so the definition is only 'who's trying to kill animals'. The National Trust for Scotland looks after heritage sites in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunter pursues and kills game animals, often on horseback with hounds in the British tradition.

clue.text: Witness is obliged to give up letter

indicators.note: giving something up means losing it, so a piece is removed from the longer word

parts.note: to be beholden is to be obliged or indebted
EN is the spelt-out name of the letter N

explanation.surface: A witness in court is forced to hand over a piece of correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to give up' removes EN, the name of the letter N, from BEHOLDEN. 'letter' looks like correspondence but is a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean to see or observe something, the older one used as a command to look.

clue.text: Revolutionary treatment for woman's trouble

indicators.note: a revolutionary treatment turns the name right round, so it is read backwards

parts.note: Sarah is a woman's name
the possessive ending of 'woman's' supplies its own letter

explanation.surface: A radical cure is offered for some female complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary treatment for' turns the name right round; the possessive 's of 'woman's' then gives its own letter at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To pester or bother someone persistently is to cause them trouble, both used as verbs.

clue.text: Hard pair pass intimidating youth

parts.note: H is the standard abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
in cricket a pair is two ducks, scores of nought, in one match, written as two Os
to pass away is to die

explanation.surface: A tough couple walk past a menacing teenager.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batter out for nought in both innings 'bags a pair': two ducks, shown as OO.
explanation.definitionFit: A hooded top gives its name to the young person wearing one, seen in Britain as a menacing figure.

clue.text: Tip-off assured after torture and coercion

indicators.note: letters that have been tortured are twisted out of shape, so they are rearranged
the tip of a word is its first letter, here knocked off the front of 'assured'

explanation.surface: An informer's confident tip comes out under torture and pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip-off' drops the A of ASSURED, leaving SSURED, and 'after torture' rearranges it. 'Tip-off' reads as a piece of secret information.
explanation.definitionFit: Duress is pressure or threats used to force someone to act against their will.

clue.text: Perhaps admitting fool's good sense?

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: say means perhaps or for example, as in 'about, say, ten'
a nit is a British word for a fool; the 's is a link meaning is

explanation.surface: A question wondering whether letting in an idiot is really wise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admitting' signals the container. Nit, short for nitwit, is everyday British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Soundness of mind means having good judgement and reasonable behaviour.

clue.text: Artist's special quality is stifled by drink

indicators.note: something stifled by another is smothered within it, so these pieces go inside

parts.note: port is a fortified wine
a trait is a distinguishing characteristic
taken as written

explanation.surface: A painter's distinctive gift is drowned in alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stifled by' puts TRAIT and IS inside PORT. The 's of 'Artist's' stands for is, linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter of likenesses is a particular kind of artist.

clue.text: Used for cleaning toilet with regular application of Flash

parts.note: loo is a British word for toilet

indicators.note: a regular application touches every other point, so alternate letters are taken

explanation.surface: Advice for cleaning the lavatory: regular squirts of a household cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regular application of' takes alternate letters of FLASH, giving FAH. Flash is a British household cleaning brand, which makes the surface plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: A dried gourd sponge is used for scrubbing the skin in the bath.

clue.text: Extrovert or retiring?

definitions.meaning: an extrovert is sociable and friendly
retiring here means leaving office, as an official about to step down

explanation.walkthrough: 'retiring' looks like the opposite of extrovert, meaning shy; here it means departing from office.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both sociable and about to leave a post, while 'retiring' usually means shy.

clue.text: Hornby novel abridged for electronic reproduction

indicators.note: an abridged work has been shortened, so most of the title is cut

parts.note: Nick Hornby wrote the novel High Fidelity

explanation.surface: A shortened Nick Hornby book is released as an audio recording.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abridged' shortens the title to its usual short form, HI-FI. Nick Hornby is an English novelist; his High Fidelity is about a record-shop owner.
explanation.definitionFit: High-quality sound equipment reproduces recorded music faithfully.

clue.text: Starts to invest dollars in China, causing alarm

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: china, from Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' for mate, is a close friend, an intimate

indicators.note: the starts of the next words are their first letters

explanation.surface: Beginning to pour dollars into China is causing financial alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to' takes I and D, put 'in' INTIMATE. China is Cockney rhyming slang: china plate = mate.
explanation.definitionFit: To frighten someone into submission is to alarm them, both used as verbs.

clue.text: Summit's head of table, perhaps

definitions.meaning: a summit is the highest point of a peak
the top of Table Mountain, above Cape Town, is one example of a peak's top

explanation.walkthrough: 'head of table' suggests the place at the end of a dining table; capitalised, Table is the mountain in South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest point of a peak is its summit, and Table Mountain's flat top is one example.

clue.text: A teen den carelessly tidied up

indicators.note: something done carelessly is messed up, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A teenager's room is half-heartedly cleaned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carelessly' rearranges A TEEN DEN; the surface suggests a scruffy teenager's room.
explanation.definitionFit: To make something neat is to tidy it, both in the past tense.

clue.text: He's eyeing and touching a peach

parts.note: on means touching or resting against, as a cup on a table
a peach and a looker are both slang for an attractive person

explanation.surface: A man ogling and groping a pretty woman.
explanation.walkthrough: A peach is old slang for a very attractive person, as is a looker.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who watches something happen, without taking part, is the one eyeing it.

clue.text: Fat tenor in "The Ring"

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: a ring is round in shape
T is a standard abbreviation for tenor in music

explanation.surface: A portly tenor stars in Wagner's Ring cycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Ring' suggests Wagner's opera cycle, which has plenty of tenors; here it simply describes a circular shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotund describes a plump, round figure, a polite word for fat.

clue.text: Partly stoned, getting jittery

indicators.note: Partly says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone half high on drugs is getting nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partly' points to the letters sitting across 'stONED GEtting'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be nervous and tense is to be anxious and jumpy.

clue.text: Chap running stamp store

indicators.note: running is taken as letters running loose, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man in charge of a shop that sells stamps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running' rearranges STAMP STORE; the whole clue also defines the person in charge of a post office.
explanation.definitionFit: The man in charge of a post office, where stamps are sold, holds this title.

clue.text: Return of first serve, inaccurately placed, gives one the game

indicators.note: a return comes back the way it went, so the letters are read backwards
the first of the following word is its first letter

parts.note: a badly placed serve ends up in the net

explanation.surface: A badly placed return of the opening serve hands a player the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return of' turns S + IN NET backwards. 'Return' and 'serve' look like tennis strokes; the surface describes the game itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennis is a racket game played over a net.

clue.text: Broken rules lead to terrible consequence

indicators.note: something broken has been knocked apart, so the letters are rearranged
the lead of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Breaking the rules brings about dire consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' rearranges RULES to RESUL, and 'lead to' takes T from 'terrible'.
explanation.definitionFit: An outcome or effect is what something ends in, its result.

clue.text: It covers the floor and wall in our house

indicators.note: to house is to contain, so the words hold the answer within them

explanation.surface: Something covering the floor and walls of our home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'house' is a verb: the words 'wall in our' house the answer in 'walL IN Our'.
explanation.definitionFit: Linoleum is a hard-wearing floor covering.

clue.text: Old jailers try to escape shift, perhaps

parts.note: a turn is a go or try, as in 'have a turn'
Escape and Shift are examples of keys on a keyboard

explanation.surface: Prisoners attempt a breakout during a shift change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'escape' and 'shift' look like a prison break, but both are keyboard keys, and 'perhaps' marks them as examples.
explanation.definitionFit: A turnkey is an old word for a jailer, the one who locks the cells.

clue.text: Cheap attempt to entrap deviant

indicators.note: to entrap is to catch and hold inside, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: a shy is an attempt, as at a coconut shy
odd means strange or deviating from the norm

explanation.surface: A tawdry attempt to snare a pervert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to entrap' signals the container. A coconut shy is a British fairground stall where you throw balls at coconuts, so a shy is a throw or attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoddy goods are poor quality and cheaply made.

clue.text: Woman in charge of automobile club

definitions.meaning: a woman at the wheel controlling a car
a golf club used for long tee shots

explanation.walkthrough: 'club' suggests a motoring club like the AA, but it is the golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: The person controlling a car is its driver, and the longest-hitting golf club has the same name.

clue.text: Run church do

parts.note: to run away is to flee
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A church social event is being organised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do' looks like a party, as in 'church do', but it is the verb meaning to cheat someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece someone is to swindle them, and 'do' is British slang for cheat.
